newsitem.title: USA: Rubin preaches free-market gospel on Asia trip.
newsitem.headline: Rubin preaches free-market gospel on Asia trip.

text.p: U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin preached the gospel of free-market capitalism during his six-day swing through Asia -- and received a generally favourable reception.

From industrial Japan to the developing Philippines to communist Vietnam, Rubin touted the economic benefits of open markets and free-flowing capital, saying they were the best way to promote growth and improve living standards worldwide.

Rubin, who returned to the United States early on Wednesday morning, gave the most complete explanation of his economic philosophy at his last stop in Asia before heading home -- at the University of Economics of Ho Chi Minh City in Vietnam.

In what could perhaps best be described as a lecture to about 100 students there, Rubin set out an eight-point blueprint for countries to follow in order to thrive in the increasingly interconnected and competitive world economy:
-- prepare the population to compete in the global economy through education, adequate health care and other measures;
-- achieve a high savings rate;
-- develop capital markets and financial institutions so as to mobilise domestic savings and attract foreign capital for use in an efficent and effective manner;
-- follow sound budget policies with small deficits;
-- reduce both formal and informal trade barriers;
-- achieve a reasonable distribution of wealth in the society by ensuring that all sectors of the population benefit from faster economic growth;
-- have true competition in all market segments;
-- protect the environment.

Rubin faced perhaps the hardest sell of his blueprint -- the self-effacing Treasury chief demurred from calling it a doctrine -- in Vietnam, America's former war-time foe now struggling to modernise its economy.
The U.S. Embassy in Hanoi -- which was just reopened in 1995 -- seemed to be cautious about the Treasury Secretary's chances for success from the outset.

Even before Rubin arrived, embassy officials were warning that Vietnam might try to embarass him by forcing him to ride around in the Cadillac used by America's last ambassador there, Graham Martin, before Washington lost the war in 1975.
In any event, that did not happen. Rubin told reporters on his way home that he did not get the feeling that the legacy of the bitter war would stand in the way of improved ties.
"The sense I had was the opposite," he said. "They're anxious to have full relations with the United States."

But he made clear that Hanoi had much to do and a way to go before that happens and urged Vietnam to press ahead with its economic reforms, saying that was the way for it to win trade concessions and financing from the United States.
Rubin said Vietnam seems to have made a "strategic decision" to move to a market economy but does not have the people familiar with such an economy to help bring that about.
He promised that the Treasury would do what it could to provide Vietnam with advice and other technical assistance to aid it in setting up a modern financial system.

The measures that countries must take to achieve that end were the focus of Rubin's discussions before he arrived in Vietnam on Sunday, at a weekend gathering in the Philippines of Asia Pacific finance ministers.

Rubin pronounced himself pleased with the results of the meeting, which set out a specific plan of action to improve the workings of the region's financial markets, and described the mood of the gathering as realistic.

No longer was there talk that the high-growth economies of Asia have discovered a new, better brand of capitalism than the United States that places a greater emphasis on government intervention in the economy and protecion of domestic industry.
"Some of them are having some problems," Rubin said. "Korea is having some problems. Thailand is having some problems. I think that created a sense of realism."
That also seems to have happened in Japan, where the economy has been mired in a near-recession for much of this decade.
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has responded by promising massive economic deregulation aimed at jump-starting the economy by freeing it from bureaucratic control.

Rubin, who met Hashimoto at the start of his trip to Asia last week, said he was impressed by the Prime Minister's commitment to liberalising the economy. But he added that it would be poltically difficult to carry that out.
